Queue API Reference¶

Back to PlussQit API Reference

This page documents pluss::Queue one method at a time, with complete behavioral prose and executable-derived outputs.

What Queue Is¶

Queue is a dynamic holder over PlussQit’s four core value types – Series, Note, Timeline, and Duration – for code that works generically across columns whose concrete type isn’t known until runtime, such as a table layer that stores Series, Note, Timeline, and Duration columns side by side. A Queue always holds exactly one of the four; kind() reports which, and invoke("method", args...) routes the method name to a method on whichever of Series, Note, Timeline, or Duration the payload actually is.

Queue is not a fifth value type with its own arithmetic rules – every operator and every invoke call forwards to the held payload’s own behavior, so Queue’s contract is almost entirely “whatever the payload would do,” plus the up-front kind bookkeeping that makes the forwarding possible without the caller needing a switch on type.

invoke() vs. the accessors: which to use¶

There are two ways to call a method through a Queue, and they are not interchangeable:

invoke("name", args)

series()/note()/timeline()/duration()

Method is picked

at run time, by a name string

at compile time, by a real C++ call

Works without knowing the kind

yes – same call shape for any kind

no – you call the accessor for the kind you expect, or it throws

Method surface reached

whatever that kind’s dispatch exposes under that name

the type’s entire public surface, exactly as its own reference documents it

Can mutate the Queue’s value

never – always returns a new Queue

yes, through the non-const overload and an in-place (_-suffixed) method

Argument checking

at run time, against the resolved method

at compile time, by ordinary C++ overload resolution

In short: reach for series()/note()/timeline()/duration() and call the method directly – q.series().mean(), q.note().strip() – whenever you already know (or are willing to assert) the kind, which is most code. It is the only way to mutate, it gives you the type’s real, full method surface with normal compile-time checking, and invoke.md’s Examples 1–4 show the same operations are reachable either way. Reach for invoke("name", args) instead only when the method name itself has to be decided at run time – generic code that doesn’t branch on kind(), a name read from configuration, or a single code path meant to apply the same operation across whichever of the four kinds a Queue happens to hold.

The two routes call the same underlying method, so they agree when both are usable:

pluss::Queue q(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0}));
const double via_invoke = q.invoke("mean").series().item<double>();
const double via_accessor = q.series().mean().item<double>();
std::cout << "via invoke(\"mean\"): " << via_invoke << '\n';
std::cout << "via series().mean(): " << via_accessor << '\n';
std::cout << "same result: " << (via_invoke == via_accessor) << '\n';

Output¶

via invoke("mean"): 2.5
via series().mean(): 2.5
same result: true

Includes¶

#include <pluss/pluss.h>
// or directly
#include <pluss/queue.h>

Practical Construction Patterns¶

Example 1. Wrap each of the four payload types. kind_name() reports which one a given Queue is actually holding. Assignment and braces make the two steps explicit: a public factory first creates the payload, and the public Queue constructor then wraps it.

const auto measurements = pluss::Queue{pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0})};
const auto labels = pluss::Queue{pluss::make_note({"a", "b"})};
const auto observed_at =
    pluss::Queue{pluss::timeline::make("1999-04-17T21:15:23Z")};
const auto timeout = pluss::Queue{pluss::duration::days(3)};

std::cout << measurements.kind_name() << ' ' << labels.kind_name() << ' '
          << observed_at.kind_name() << ' ' << timeout.kind_name() << '\n';

Output¶

Series Note Timeline Duration

See construction for every constructor form.

Coverage¶

This reference covers the canonical public surface:

  • construction: four constructors, one per payload type, each with a copy and a move overload – construction

  • identifying the payload: the Kind enum, kind

  • typed access back to the payload: accessors (series(), note(), timeline(), duration())

  • structural introspection: state (defined(), dim(), numel())

  • generic templated access: generic-access (is<T>(), as<T>())

  • a visitor over whichever payload is held: visit

  • calling a method on the held payload by name: invoke

  • every public operator call form: operators

  • the static ternary selector: where

  • printing: stream (operator<<)

Each distinct method has its own page. Queue::Arg (the implicit-conversion wrapper invoke’s argument list accepts) is documented inline on invoke rather than on its own page, since it has no behavior of its own beyond holding one argument.
